/home/user/adss-2026-09-07, on branch claude/adss-slice-04-revenue-per-order-month.

FINDING: ADR 0012 records a change to ADR 0002 that was not made and, under the ADR rules, cannot be
FILE: /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/adr/0012-the-bridge-protects-measures-and-not-the-attributes-beside-them.md:71
DETAIL: ADR 0012's Decision Outcome states: "The property is proved for measures, **the limit of that proof is written into ADR 0002's contract as a third query-time rule**, and a question whose answer query aggregates a peripheral's numeric column is refused by the question checker."

It was not written into ADR 0002. `docs/adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md:112` still reads "**Two** rules follow from the contract and are written down because they are query-time traps" and still lists exactly two (INNER vs LEFT on an inherited key; a ratio is `sum(a)/sum(b)`). The only edit this slice made to ADR 0002 was inside its Confirmation section (lines 160-165).

And it could not have been written there. `docs/adr/README.md:3-4` — "A record is **superseded by a new file, never edited**" — with exactly one exception, README:8-11, the Confirmation section. Line 112 is in the decision body, so amending it is forbidden; superseding ADR 0002 was not done either.

ADR 0012's own Consequences section contradicts its Decision Outcome on the same point: line 79 says "ADR 0002 already publishes two query-time rules and neither covers this one; a third would be true, unread and unenforced."

The result is that the bridge's published contract — the thing ADR 0002 says "every consumer is written against" — is silent about a rule every consumer must now obey. `.claude/skills/dar/SKILL.md:52` already announces "Three consequences at query time" against ADR 0002's two.
WHY IT MATTERS: A reader who follows ADR 0012 to ADR 0002 to find the third rule will not find it, and a reader of ADR 0002 alone will believe the contract is complete. The fix that the record implies is the one the ADR rules forbid, so the decision as written cannot be carried out — it needs a different home (see the conventions.md §10 finding) or a superseding record.

Your job is to try to DESTROY this finding. Read the actual code. Run the actual command or
test if that settles it. Look for the reason the finding is wrong: a check elsewhere that
already catches it, a documented decision that accepts it on purpose (docs/adr/,
docs/deviations.md, docs/conventions.md, the question documents), an invariant that makes the
bad input impossible, or a simple misreading.

Do NOT modify any file. If you must experiment, copy to a scratch directory.

Return isReal=true ONLY if the defect genuinely exists in this head and is not already
recorded as a known limitation. confidence is 0-10: how sure you are, having tried to break
your own conclusion. If isReal, give the smallest correct fix.

2	status: accepted
3	date: 2026-09-08
4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
5	slice: 4
6	---
7	
8	# The bridge protects a measure and not the attribute it was made from, so a question may not aggregate a peripheral's number
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	D-0001 puts every process into one shared `dar__uss`, departing from the blueprint's
13	no-cross-dependency rule. Its entire justification, written in slice 1 and carried unexercised
14	through three slices, is that *the fan trap R2 exists to prevent cannot occur in it* — because
15	keys inherit along many-to-one edges and measures do not.
16	
17	Slice 4 is the first slice with two grains, so it is the first that can test that. It half holds.
18	
19	**The measures are safe, structurally, and this is the first demonstration of it.** Over the real
20	two-grain bridge — 830 order rows and 2155 line rows — every shape returns the truth:
21	
22	| query | freight | revenue |
23	|---|---|---|
24	| both measures, whole bridge, no filter, no join | **64,942.69** ✓ | **1,265,793.0395** ✓ |
25	| both, per order month, joined to `_calendar` (3794 rows) | **64,942.69** ✓ | **1,265,793.0395** ✓ |
26	
27	2155 line rows carry `order_key`, and freight does not move. That is what D-0001 has been
28	asserting, and it is now a measurement.
29	
30	**The peripheral is not safe, and the query that breaks it is not exotic.** It is one join — the
31	same join `q01` and `q02` already write:
32	
33	```sql
34	SELECT sum(o.freight_charge)
35	FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
36	INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
37	WHERE b._event = 'ordered';
38	-- 207,306.10 against a true 64,942.69. Once per LINE.
39	```
40	
41	`freight_charge` is a **published column of the order peripheral**. So the rule generalises to
42	something D-0001 never said:
43	
44	> Any `NUMBER` attribute that is also a measure's source appears **twice** in `dar__uss` — once
45	> as an additive measure on its owning stage, protected by a typed null on every other branch,
46	> and once as a plain attribute on its peripheral, protected by nothing. `FREIGHT_CHARGE`,
47	> `SHIP_LAG_DAYS` and `REVENUE` are all in that position.
48	
49	**And it was already live at slice 3, undetected.** On the warehouse as shipped in PR #3, before
50	any line existed, the same query returns **128,897.71** against 64,942.69 — because `ORDER` had
51	two events, so the bridge already had two rows per order. Slice 4 does not introduce the trap. It
52	raises it from 1.98× to 3.19× and makes it reachable from another entity's stage, which is what a
53	fan trap actually is.
54	
55	## Decision Drivers
56	
57	* the property D-0001 rests on is demonstrated or the deviation's argument is not carried
58	* what the demonstration does *not* cover is stated, rather than left for a reader to discover
59	* the trap is kept out of what this system publishes, since it cannot be kept out of SQL
60	* nothing legitimate is removed to achieve it
61	
62	## Considered Options
63	
64	* Stop publishing a numeric attribute on a peripheral when it is also a measure's source
65	* Publish it, and add a query-time rule to the bridge's contract
66	* Publish it, add the rule, **and refuse a question that breaks it**
67	
68	## Decision Outcome
69	
70	Chosen: **the third.** The property is proved for measures, the limit of that proof is written
71	into ADR 0002's contract as a third query-time rule, and a question whose answer query aggregates
72	a peripheral's numeric column is **refused** by the question checker.
73	
74	**Why not remove the column.** A numeric attribute on a peripheral is legitimately useful — it is
75	how a reader filters "orders whose freight was over 100" or sorts a table by it. Removing it to
76	prevent a bad aggregate would break the good use to prevent the bad one, and would make the
77	peripheral a worse description of the entity than the entity has.
78	
79	**Why a rule alone is not enough.** ADR 0002 already publishes two query-time rules and neither
80	covers this one; a third would be true, unread and unenforced. This system's own position, stated
81	in ADR 0006 and ADR 0008, is that a failure which is invisible gets refused where it can be seen.
82	
83	**What can actually be enforced.** Not "no reader writes a bad query" — a bridge does not stop a
84	bad query, it makes the good one natural, and the honest form of that claim is narrower than it
85	sounds. But every number this system *publishes* goes through a question's `uss.sql`, and those
86	are files this repository owns and already checks. So: an answer query may not apply an aggregate
87	to a column of a peripheral. It must aggregate `_measure__…` columns, which are the ones the
88	bridge protects. That is checkable, it is checked, and it stops the trap entering the artefacts
89	anybody reads.
90	
91	The rule has one deliberate hole: a question may still aggregate a peripheral's column if it does
92	so outside `uss.sql`, and a person at a SQL prompt can do whatever they like. That is not a gap
93	this decision can close and pretending otherwise would be the false comfort D-0001 has been
94	running on.
95	
96	### D-0001 does not close
97	
98	Its exit condition, quoted whole, is: *"A second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of
99	the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it."* That has not happened. Slice 4
100	adds a fourth question read by one more persona, and a persona is not a consumer needing
101	isolation — nothing here needs a different shape of the bridge and nothing must be hidden from
102	anybody. Closing the entry now would be closing it for a reason that is not its own exit
103	condition, which is how a register becomes decoration.
104	
105	What changes is the register's **Why**. It has said since slice 1 that the fan trap "cannot occur"
106	in the shared structure. That is true of the measures and false of the peripherals, and the entry
107	now says which, with the number.
108	
109	## Consequences
110	
111	* Good, because the argument D-0001 has been carried on for three slices is measured rather than
112	  asserted, and the measurement is repeated on every build
113	* Good, because the half that does *not* hold is written down with the query that breaks it and
114	  the number it returns, rather than being discovered by somebody trusting the entry
115	* Good, because the trap cannot enter a published answer, which is where it would be believed
116	* Bad, because the refusal is a text rule over SQL, and a sufficiently determined query defeats
117	  it — an aggregate spelled across a subquery, for instance. It raises the cost of the mistake
118	  from zero to deliberate, which is what the other refusals in this system do too
119	* Bad, because a question that genuinely wants a peripheral's number aggregated — "the largest
120	  freight on any order" — now has to model it as a measure. That is more honest and more typing,
121	  and it is the same trade ADR 0008 made
122	
123	## Confirmation
124	
125	`tests/test_fan_out.py` asserts the fan-out property directly, on the neutral fixture's two
126	grains: a parent's measure summed over a bridge containing its children equals the parent's own
127	total, the finer measure is right in the same scan, the coarser measure is null on every finer row
128	while the inherited **key** is not, and — the falsifiable half — the parent's total does not move
129	when a parent gains children. It runs the generated SQL against a warehouse it builds, rather than
130	reading the SQL for substrings, because a substring assertion would pass a generator that emitted
131	the right nulls in the wrong branch.
132	
133	That it can fail is measured rather than assumed. The generator was mutated so a measure inherits
134	along an edge exactly as a key does — carried in the CTE that walks the edge, selected by the
135	stage, and treated as the branch's own. It emits SQL DuckDB accepts, and the four assertions fail
136	together: 402.00 in place of 150.75, three parent measures on the three child rows in place of
137	none, and 904.50 against 402.00 when five children are added to a parent whose size did not
138	change. A fifth test — the peripheral trap below — passes under that mutation, which is correct:
139	the mutation is in the bridge and the trap is not.
140	
141	A generated data check, one per measure, asserts it is null on every row of every **event** that
142	does not own it — the mechanism rather than the number, on the warehouse that was actually built.
143	By event and not by stage: two events on one entity share a stage, so a per-stage check would let
144	an order's shipment measure sit on its placement row and report nothing, and that is the likelier
145	defect since every branch of the union comes off the same stage's CTE. `tests/test_measure_checks.py`
146	runs each check against a bridge built to fail it, including that case.
147	
148	`tests/test_questions.py` asserts that an answer query aggregating a peripheral's column is
149	refused, and that the same aggregate over a `_measure__` column is accepted. Every question in
150	this repository is run through the refusal, so the rule is enforced rather than published.
151	
152	**It is not the text rule the Consequences above anticipated.** The refusal reads the engine's own
153	parse tree for the answer query and the engine's own list of aggregate functions, so a `cast()`
154	around the sum, a sum written as a window, a subquery, and an aggregate nobody thought to list are
155	all caught — three of which a text rule would have missed, and the third is why the list is not
156	kept by hand. Four mutations of the refusal were run and all four fail the suite.
157	
158	It is stricter than the trap requires, in two places worth naming. `count(*)` over the bridge is
159	refused, because it counts measurement events rather than the thing asked about — two events on
160	one entity and it doubles. And an aggregate over a `DISTINCT` peripheral column cannot be
161	multiplied by a fan-out and is refused anyway: narrowing the rule to the aggregates that can
162	actually be wrong would be a rule nobody could apply without already knowing which those are.
163	
164	What still defeats it is narrower than the Consequences claim: not a subquery, but an answer that
165	never writes an aggregate at all, or one that aliases a measure to a new name and aggregates the
166	alias — which is refused too, so the honest statement is that the rule is over-strict at the edge
167	rather than porous there.
168	
169	What is **not** confirmed: that no reader ever writes the bad query at a prompt. Nothing can
170	confirm that, and the register now says so instead of implying otherwise.

     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-07
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 1
     6	---
     7	
     8	# DAR is one generated Unified Star Schema: an event bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys, one peripheral per entity, one dense calendar
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	DAR is the layer a person reads. The blueprint says it is volatile and generated (R4), and the
    13	Unified Star Schema is the shape chosen for it: one *bridge* holding a row per measurement event,
    14	one *peripheral* per entity holding its current state, and one calendar every process is dated
    15	against. This record fixes what the generator emits, because every question, every page and every
    16	future consumer is written against those column names and will not survive them changing.
    17	
    18	Three things about the source make the shape less obvious than the description sounds.
    19	
    20	**Fan-out.** The USS description says keys and measures propagate downward along many-to-one
    21	relationships. Keys can. Measures cannot: if a parent's measure were copied onto every child row
    22	that points at it, summing that measure would multiply it by the number of children. That is the
    23	classic fan trap, and avoiding it is the entire reason a bridge exists rather than one wide join.
    24	
    25	**History.** DAB keeps a version of every entity row. A question about something that *happened*
    26	and a question about a state as it was *observed* are different questions and need different rows,
    27	but they belong in one table, because the whole value of the bridge is that two processes can be
    28	summed and compared on one calendar.
    29	
    30	**What the generator is allowed to read.** Two observations constrain this hard, and both were
    31	made against the real engine on DuckDB rather than reasoned about. `<entity>_focal` and
    32	`<entity>_idfr` are created but never populated — a generator that joined to them would produce
    33	empty results and no error. And `view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at
    34	all, despite its name; its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. A generator built on
    35	the names alone would be wrong in both directions.
    36	
    37	There is a fourth thing, and it is the one this slice cannot demonstrate. The argument that one
    38	shared bridge is safe rests on the walk over many-to-one edges. Slice 1 has one entity and no
    39	relationships, so the walk has zero edges and nothing inherits. The property is asserted here and
    40	first exercised in slice 2.
    41	
    42	## Decision Drivers
    43	
    44	* a `sum()` over the bridge is right without the reader knowing how the model is shaped
    45	* one calendar, so two processes can be compared
    46	* a published column contract that a model change *extends* rather than rearranges
    47	* deterministic output: the same declarations always produce the same SQL
    48	* nothing silently missing
    49	
    50	## Considered Options
    51	
    52	* An event bridge with one stage per (entity, event), keys inherited and measures owned
    53	* One bridge row per entity instance, with measures joined on
    54	* A hand-written star schema per question
    55	* Reading DAB's relationship views for the inherited keys
    56	
    57	## Decision Outcome
    58	
    59	Chosen option: **an event-grained bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys.**
    60	
    61	*Keys inherit; measures do not.* A stage carries the key of every entity it reaches by walking
    62	many-to-one edges, and a measure is non-null only on the stage of the (entity, event) that owns
    63	it. Every other branch of the union emits a typed `NULL` in that column. This is what makes
    64	`sum()` additive at any grain the reader chooses, and it is proved by a test rather than trusted:
    65	a fixture with two parents and three children, where `sum(_measure__parent__…)` must still be the
    66	parent total and not three times it.
    67	
    68	*One row per measurement event.* A transaction stage reads `dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest
    69	version in which the event's date is set, and dates the row by that attribute. An unshipped order
    70	therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
    71	remember. A state stage reads the same history view, dates rows by `eff_tmstp`, and marks the
    72	latest version per key `_is_current`. Both kinds land in the same table with the same columns,
    73	which is what lets them be compared.
    74	
    75	*The generator reads `view_<entity>_hist` and the relationship pair objects, and nothing else.*
    76	Not `_focal`, which is empty. Not `_with_rel`, which does not carry what its name implies. Reading
    77	the current view instead of the history view would also lose `_observed_at`, which is how a bridge
    78	row carries its own provenance back to the DAS load that produced it.
    79	
    80	The rejected options each fail on one of the drivers. One row per entity instance with measures
    81	joined on is the fan trap, restated as a design. A hand-written star per question abandons R4 and
    82	puts the layer's correctness in a person's hands, every time, forever. Reading the relationship
    83	*views* rather than the pair objects is the subtle one: those views rank pairs by effective
    84	timestamp and keep the open rows, and our effective timestamp is the moment DAS observed the row,
    85	so a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely — rows silently missing from the
    86	bridge, with the query still running and the total merely smaller.
    87	
    88	### The column contract
    89	
    90	`dar__uss._bridge`:
    91	
    92	| column | type | null | meaning |
    93	|---|---|---|---|
    94	| `_stage` | VARCHAR | no | the entity this row is a row *of* |
    95	| `_event` | VARCHAR | no | the event, lower-cased: `placed`, `shipped`, `observed` |
    96	| `_event_date` | DATE | no | the day it happened, or the day the state was observed; joins `_calendar.date_key` |
    97	| `_is_current` | BOOLEAN | no | always true on a transaction stage; the latest version per key on a state stage |
    98	| `_observed_at` | TIMESTAMP | no | the DAB `eff_tmstp` behind this row, which is the DAS `extracted_at` |
    99	| `<entity>_key` | VARCHAR | own key no, inherited yes | one per entity in model order |
   100	| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | BIGINT for a count, DECIMAL(28,8) for a sum | non-null only on the owning stage | one per declared measure, in model order |
   101	
   102	`dar__uss.<entity>` is a peripheral **table**, one row per key, key first and attributes in
   103	declaration order. Tables rather than views, so what DAR served is exactly what the build log

+DAR is the layer a person reads. The blueprint says it is volatile and generated (R4), and the

+that points at it, summing that measure would multiply it by the number of children. That is the
+classic fan trap, and avoiding it is the entire reason a bridge exists rather than one wide join.

+**History.** DAB keeps a version of every entity row. A question about something that *happened*
+and a question about a state as it was *observed* are different questions and need different rows,
+but they belong in one table, because the whole value of the bridge is that two processes can be
+summed and compared on one calendar.

+shared bridge is safe rests on the walk over many-to-one edges. Slice 1 has one entity and no

+* a `sum()` over the bridge is right without the reader knowing how the model is shaped
+* one calendar, so two processes can be compared
+* a published column contract that a model change *extends* rather than rearranges
+* deterministic output: the same declarations always produce the same SQL
+* nothing silently missing

+## Considered Options

+* An event bridge with one stage per (entity, event), keys inherited and measures owned
+* One bridge row per entity instance, with measures joined on
+* A hand-written star schema per question

+
+Chosen option: **an event-grained bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys.**

+many-to-one edges, and a measure is non-null only on the stage of the (entity, event) that owns

# DAR — data according to the requirements

One bridge, one peripheral per entity, one calendar. **Nothing here is hand-written**, and a
wrong name is fixed in the model and regenerated. An edit to generated output is lost on the
next generation, and until then the code and the model quietly disagree.

## The shape

```
dab/uss.yaml        the declarations: events, their dates, their measures
dar/uss/*.sql       generated and committed
```

`uv run adss dar generate` writes them; `--check` fails if the committed SQL is not what the
model produces; `uv run adss dar build` runs them.

## The column contract

Everything downstream is written against these names and will not survive them changing. A
model change **appends**; it never rearranges.

| column | what it is |
|---|---|
| `_stage` | the entity this row is a row *of* |
| `_event` | the event, lower-cased |
| `_event_date` | joins `_calendar.date_key` |
| `_is_current` | always true on a transaction stage |
| `_observed_at` | the DAB effective timestamp, which is the DAS extraction time |
| `<entity>_key` | one per entity, in model order |
| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | one per measure; **non-null only on the owning stage** |

## The one rule that matters most

**Keys inherit; measures do not.** A stage carries the key of every entity it reaches along
many-to-one relationships, and a measure is non-null only on the stage that owns it. Copying a
parent's measure onto its children multiplies it when summed — that is the fan trap, and
avoiding it is the entire reason there is a bridge rather than one wide join.

Slice 4 measured it on two grains rather than asserting it: 2,155 line rows carry an order key
and the order's freight stays at 64,942.69. `tests/test_fan_out.py` is that measurement, and a
generated check per measure repeats it on every build.

**The half that is false.** The bridge protects the measure *column*. It protects nothing on a
peripheral — and a numeric attribute that is also a measure's source is published in **both**
places. `sum(o.freight_charge)` over `_bridge ⨝ order` returns 207,306.10 against a true
64,942.69: once per line. It is one join and one sum, and it looks exactly like an answer.

Three consequences at query time, none of which the schema can enforce:

- A join on the row's own `_stage` key may be `INNER`. A join on an **inherited** key must be
  `LEFT`.
- A ratio is `sum(a) / sum(b)` at query time. It is never a stored measure: an average of
  averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at.
- **Aggregate `_measure__` columns and nothing else.** A question's `uss.sql` is refused if it
  applies any aggregate to a peripheral's column, or writes `count(*)` over the bridge — which
  counts measurement events rather than the thing asked about. Checked on the engine's parse
  tree, so a cast, a window or a subquery does not get past it. ADR 0012.

## Adding a measure

Add it to `dab/uss.yaml` under its event, with a **definition** — the glossary copies these
verbatim and never composes one. Name it `<descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>`, entity plural, no
scope or aggregation words: `placed_orders_count`, never `total_orders`. Then regenerate.

| Rule | Why | Severity |

The drift check is what stops the committed copy becoming a second truth nothing compares against the model. Any formatting the generator's output needs must happen *inside* the generator, or every regeneration produces a spurious diff. | Hard rule |

## 9. The warehouse has exactly one writer

The lock is **per process**. Within one process every connection shares an instance, so a
second open succeeds; across processes the second is refused. That distinction is the whole of
this section, and getting it backwards costs an afternoon.

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| This process must not hold the warehouse open while a separate process is asked to write to it. `require_detached` enforces it rather than asking anyone to remember. | The modelling engine is a separate process. While we hold the file it cannot take the lock, and it reports that as `daana framework is not installed on the remote database` — which is not what went wrong. Reproduced with DuckDB alone, no engine involved. | Hard rule |
| Every destination opens the warehouse with `read_only=True`. | A read-only handle still holds the process lock, so a page left open blocks the next build; read-only at least keeps a reader from writing. | Hard rule |
| `daana framework is not installed on the remote database` means **the file is busy**. | The real lock error is swallowed and does not appear even at debug level. Anyone meeting this message will otherwise spend an afternoon reinstalling a framework that is already installed. | Hard rule |

A question is the unit of delivery, and it is a **data file**, not code. That is what keeps the
acceptance test free of business vocabulary (§6) and what lets the same artefact serve the test,
the page and the reader.

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|

| `question.md` front matter carries the measure, dimensions, aggregation, time grain, persona, status, and the definitions the question depends on. Its prose carries the story and the W's. | A question that needs a conversation to be answerable is a Stage 1 question, and the whole point is to reach Stage 3. | Hard rule |
| A question **references** definitions; it never restates them. Every reference must resolve to something `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` defines, and the machinery proves it. | Blueprint B8. A restated definition is a second definition, and it will be the one that is out of date. | Hard rule |
| A question that needs a term the model does not define is **blocked**, and the model change comes first. | This is the methodology working: a question the model cannot answer has found a gap in the model, which is what asking it was for. | Hard rule |
| The staged query reads `das__staged.<table>__current` and must not mention `dab` or `dar__uss`. The USS query reads `dar__uss` only. Both halves are checked. | Independence is the whole value. A staged query that consults DAB is a transcription of the other one wearing a disguise; and the page runs the USS query verbatim, so one that reached past DAR would render, pass, and be exactly the invisible dependency the flow rules exist to prevent. | Hard rule |
| The front matter's dimensions must appear in the **USS** query. They are DAR's names; the control query says the same thing in the source's words. | That difference is what makes the control independent rather than a transcription. Requiring the same spelling in both would force one to be written from the other. | Hard rule |

## 11. When a rule does not fit

Rules are aimed at cases; a case the rule was not aimed at is not a violation. Cheapest recourse
first:

1. **Clarify this page.** If the rule was ambiguous, say what it means and add the case. The
   clarification is in force immediately, for everyone.
2. **Register a deviation.** If the rule is right and this one place genuinely cannot follow it,
   add an entry to [deviations.md](deviations.md) — rule, reason, cost, exit condition — and an
   ADR explaining the decision.
3. **Change the rule.** If it is wrong, supersede the ADR that established it and edit this page.
   A rule nobody follows should be deleted rather than left as a reason to distrust the rest.

What is not on the list: a quiet exception. That is how a system of conventions turns into a set
of stories about why each file is the way it is.

Slice 4 is the first with two grains, so it is the first that can test what D-0001 has been
carried on since slice 1: that the fan trap cannot occur in one shared star schema. It half
holds, and the half that does not was already live before this slice.

The measures are safe, structurally, and this is the first demonstration of it. Over 830 order
rows and 2155 line rows, freight is 64,942.69 and revenue 1,265,793.0395 -- whole bridge, no
filter, and per order month alike. 2155 line rows carry an order key and freight does not move.

The peripherals are not safe, and the query that breaks them is one join -- the same join two
shipped questions already write. sum(order.freight_charge) over the bridge returns 207,306.10
against a true 64,942.69, because freight_charge is a published column of the order peripheral.
So any NUMBER attribute that is also a measure's source is in dar__uss twice: once protected by
a typed null on every branch that does not own it, once protected by nothing. Freight, ship lag
and revenue are all in that position.

And it was live at slice 3 already, undetected: on the warehouse shipped in PR #3, before any
line existed, the same query returns 128,897.71, because ORDER had two events. Slice 4 does not
introduce the trap; it raises it from 1.98x to 3.19x and makes it reachable from another
entity's stage, which is what a fan trap actually is.

Removing the column was rejected -- a number on a peripheral is how a reader filters or sorts,
and breaking the good use to prevent the bad one makes the peripheral a worse description than
the entity has. A query-time rule alone was rejected too: ADR 0002 already publishes two and a
third would be true, unread and unenforced.

What can be enforced is narrower and worth having. Every number this system publishes goes
through a question's answer query, and those are files this repository owns and already checks.
So an answer query may not aggregate a peripheral's column; it aggregates the measure columns,
which are the ones the bridge protects. A person at a SQL prompt can still do as they like, and
the register now says that rather than implying otherwise.

D-0001 does not close. Its exit condition is a second consumer needing isolation, and a fourth
question read by one more persona is not that. Closing it now would be closing it for a reason
that is not its own exit condition, which is how a register becomes decoration. What changes is
its Why, which has said "cannot occur" since slice 1 and now says which half.
